title: Teresa of Kolkata (1910–1997)
hook: a teacher leaves her convent to care for the dying poor, and writes later of long spiritual darkness
tomorrow: Camp 2 close: the cloud of witnesses (Hebrews 12:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maximilian Kolbe, who died in a stranger's place in Auschwitz. Your line was he stepped forward. Where did you step forward, even a little? Day ninety-five.

September 1946. A nun in her thirties is on a crowded, overnight train from Calcutta up into the hills of Darjeeling, heading for a retreat. For nearly twenty years she's taught geography and history to girls at a convent school, behind walls, in a city full of people sleeping and dying on the pavements outside. Somewhere on that train, she said later, she heard a call inside her call: leave the convent, and go to live with the poorest of the poor. She was born in Skopje, as Anjezë Bojaxhiu. When she became a nun she took her name from a saint you met two days ago, Thérèse of Lisieux. Today: Teresa of Kolkata.
screen: `A TRAIN TO DARJEELING, 1946.` → `A CALL INSIDE HER CALL.` → `NAMED FOR THÉRÈSE.`

segments.voice: It took her two years to get permission. In 1948 she put on a cheap white sari with blue borders, took some basic nursing training, and walked into the slums with almost nothing. A few of her former students joined her. In 1950 the Church approved her new order, the Missionaries of Charity. Soon after, she opened a home for the dying in an old building beside the Kali temple in Kalighat, where people found in the street could die washed, fed, and held, whatever their religion. She called it Nirmal Hriday, pure heart. The order spread to cities all over the world. In 1979 she received the Nobel Peace Prize. Here's the part few people knew until after she died in 1997. Her letters, published in 2007, showed that for close to fifty years, from around the time she started this work, she felt God's absence. She wrote of darkness and emptiness, and that she no longer felt the presence she'd felt on that train. She kept going anyway, every day, on the floor with the sick. She had critics too, over the medical care in her homes and over some of her funding, and people still argue about that. In 2016 Pope Francis declared her a saint. Her way was close to her namesake's. She is often quoted as saying most of us can't do great things, only small things with great love. Catholics see in her the words of Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."
screen: `A WHITE SARI, INTO THE SLUMS.` · `A HOME FOR THE DYING.` · `FIFTY YEARS OF DARKNESS.` · `CRITICS, AND A SAINT.` · then, large: `SMALL THINGS WITH GREAT LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see the person in front of you. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next person you'll actually be face to face with today. A coworker. A cashier. Someone at home. Picture their face, and try to see them as she tried to see the dying on the pavement: not a task, not a problem, a person. Notice one thing about them you usually miss. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Nirmal Hriday. Bengali for pure heart, the home where Teresa of Kolkata let the dying be washed, fed, and held.
Your line: small things with great love. Today, when you meet that person, really look at them, and do one small thing for them well. Day ninety-five.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of St. Teresa of Calcutta on September 5, the day she died; the Missionaries of Charity continue her work in homes for the dying, the sick and the abandoned around the world, and volunteers often serve alongside them.

original.note: Bengali: pure heart, the name of her home for the dying at Kalighat.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint who always felt close to God.
what it means: a woman who served the dying for decades while feeling, most of that time, that God was far away.
what a scholar hears: the letters in Come Be My Light (2007) show her darkness began around 1948 and lasted, with brief exceptions, until her death.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'nobody knew' about her darkness softened to 'few people knew' (her confessors knew); 'a decade later' replaced by the cited 2007; the Matthew 25:40 paraphrase, which echoed modern copyrighted wording, replaced with the Douay-Rheims text.

Dates: born August 26, 1910 in Skopje; 'call within a call' September 10, 1946; left Loreto 1948; Missionaries of Charity approved October 1950; Nirmal Hriday opened 1952 at Kalighat; Nobel Peace Prize 1979; died September 5, 1997; canonized September 4, 2016. Confirm.
Birth name given as Anjezë (Agnes) Gonxhe Bojaxhiu; the script says 'Anjezë Bojaxhiu'. Confirm spelling.
She took the name Teresa after Thérèse of Lisieux (choosing the Spanish spelling because another nun already had 'Thérèse'): confirm.
Bengali নির্মল হৃদয় and the pronunciation 'NIR-mol HRI-doy' should be checked by a Bengali speaker.
'Small things with great love' is widely attributed to her in varying wording; paraphrased, not quoted.
Critics (medical care in homes, funding sources) mentioned in one sentence without taking sides; confirm the Keeper is comfortable with this.
Matthew 25:40 now quoted from the Douay-Rheims (the earlier paraphrase echoed modern copyrighted wording); confirm.
